meta.notes: Primary ICP from context is 'Large EU Employers Using High-Risk HR AI' (deployers), although the idea's stated beachhead is HR-tech vendors (providers); unknowns mostly concern vendors, so evidence covers both. Prospects target the primary ICP: 19 companies (below the 20 target). Many corporate sites (Allianz, SAP, Bayer, Forvia, Heineken, ST) block the fetcher, so several German employers rest only on a news item (Lucca transparency index via borncity); only 1 contact (Ubisoft CPO) could be taken from a company's own page. No job postings for AI Act roles at HR-tech vendors were found via search. Cost figures are consultancy estimates. Regulatory timeline as of Nov 2026: Omnibus (Reg. 2026/1744) in force; Annex III from 2 Dec 2027. Unverifiable pages (Littler via allwork.space, techzine, corporatecomplianceinsights, verdantix, dataprotectionreport) were not cited.

evidence.title: Digital AI Omnibus Delays Key Deadlines, Introduces New Rules (Cooley)
evidence.quote: On 24 July 2026, the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) was published in the Official Journal of the European Union … High-risk AI (Annex III stand-alone systems – e.g. employment, education, law enforcement) | 2 August 2026 | 2 December 2027 (16-month deferral)
evidence.statement: The Digital Omnibus on AI is law; Annex III high-risk obligations (including employment AI) now apply from 2 December 2027, not August 2026.

evidence.title: Digital AI Omnibus Delays Key Deadlines, Introduces New Rules (Cooley)
evidence.quote: The grace period under Article 111(2) operates at the type and model level. If at least one unit of a given type and model was lawfully placed on the market before the applicable compliance date, other units of the same type and model may continue to be placed on the market without additional obligations, provided the design remains materially unchanged.
evidence.statement: Under Article 111(2), high-risk systems already on the market before the compliance date can keep being placed on the market without new obligations unless their design changes materially.

evidence.title: EU's AI Act Delays Let High-Risk Systems Dodge Oversight (Tech Policy Press)
evidence.quote: pointed to AI used in hiring systems, explicitly classified as high-risk under the AI Act, as an example. If such a system is placed on the market before December 2, 2027, “it may remain outside the AI Act indefinitely, unless it is substantially altered after that date.”
evidence.statement: A former AI Act co-negotiator says hiring AI placed on the market before 2 December 2027 may stay outside the Act indefinitely unless substantially altered, which weakens the compliance deadline for incumbent HR-tech products.

evidence.title: Digital AI Omnibus Delays Key Deadlines, Introduces New Rules (Cooley)
evidence.quote: The Omnibus extends existing small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) exemptions from certain administrative requirements to small mid-cap enterprises (SMCs) … SMCs will benefit from streamlined documentation requirements and additional flexibility in post-market monitoring.
evidence.statement: SME relief now extends to small mid-caps, with streamlined documentation and lighter post-market monitoring, reducing the documentation burden for many HR-tech vendors.

evidence.title: What does EU AI Act compliance cost: realistic numbers per organisation type
evidence.quote: A mid-sized organisation with one or more candidate high-risk systems should budget 25,000 to 100,000 euros. A large enterprise, or a provider that places high-risk AI on the market itself, quickly reaches 100,000 to 500,000 euros or more, including conformity work and ongoing governance.
evidence.statement: A practitioner estimate (mid-2026) puts year-one AI Act cost at EUR 25k-100k for mid-sized organisations with candidate high-risk systems and EUR 100k-500k+ for providers of high-risk AI.

evidence.title: What does EU AI Act compliance cost: realistic numbers per organisation type
evidence.quote: AI governance platforms (registers, workflows, monitoring, evidence management) are almost always sold as annual licences. Entry prices of international vendors start around 10,000 to 20,000 euros per year; enterprise implementations run to 50,000 to 100,000 euros per year or more.
evidence.statement: AI governance platforms are sold as annual licences from about EUR 10k-20k per year at entry level, in line with the idea's EUR 500-2,500/month hypothesis.

evidence.title: What does EU AI Act compliance cost: realistic numbers per organisation type
evidence.quote: An honest note: an SME with five AI systems is often well served by a structured register in existing tooling. Buying software before the inventory is finished is the most common budgeting mistake.
evidence.statement: The same source says a smaller organisation is often well served by a register in existing tooling rather than dedicated software.

evidence.title: What does EU AI Act compliance cost: realistic numbers per organisation type
evidence.quote: For most organisations, however, the bill arrives from a different direction first: procurement teams demanding AI Act evidence in tenders, clients asking for contractual assurances
evidence.statement: Procurement teams demanding AI Act evidence in tenders, and clients asking for contractual assurances, are described as the first cost most organisations face.

evidence.statement: One (non-HR) startup example reports eighteen months and over EUR 200,000 spent preparing for AI Act compliance.

summary.statement: Practitioner estimates put year-one AI Act cost at EUR 25k-100k for mid-sized organisations with candidate high-risk systems and EUR 100k-500k+ for providers of high-risk AI; these are estimates, not HR-tech-vendor measurements.
Each AI/security procurement questionnaire takes 10-40 hours of combined effort without automation.
HR-tech SaaS providers typically have to write quality-management documentation from scratch.
The Omnibus extends streamlined documentation to SMEs and small mid-caps, which lowers the burden for many HR-tech vendors.
No source measured hours or spend at an actual HR-tech vendor; the per-vendor cost remains unmeasured.
HR-tech vendors use HR-specific bias-audit and governance tools: Warden AI (Beamery, PageUp, Whippy) and FairNow (Dayforce, Ashby, Humanly, Plum).
Large vendors build it in-house: Workday holds ISO 42001 certification and publishes AI Fact Sheets; TestGorilla runs its own ISO 42001-aligned AI management system.
Horizontal platforms (Vanta, OneTrust, Modulos, Credo AI, Holistic AI) cover AI Act classification, registry and evidence.
The boring answer is spreadsheets, Word templates and ad hoc questionnaire answers.
On the employer side, governance ownership is often missing: only 32% of HR leaders report a named AI governance role, and legal is often brought into HR AI procurement too late.
Governance tools sell as annual licences from about EUR 10k-20k a year at entry level; IBM watsonx.governance lists from $3,500/month.
Many European HR departments operate without an AI budget.
No evidence was found on who owns AI Act compliance inside HR-tech vendors or what they budget.
EU enterprise buyers are adding AI Act question blocks to standard vendor assessments, and HR-tech vendors report procurement and legal teams already asking.
An HR-tech CEO says enterprise customers increasingly want independent evidence from providers.
Demand comes from large employers: 21 of Germany's 25 largest employers use applicant software with AI functions.
No source gives a count of requests per vendor per month.
Bias audits alone do not replace the Act's conformity assessment, as an audited vendor states.
A competitor notes that Vanta refers customers to a specialist for CE marking.
Against the gap: HR-specific tools already exist, and FairNow was acquired by AuditBoard, which shows large GRC vendors moving in.
For smaller organisations a register in existing tooling is often enough.
No buyer-voice complaints (reviews, forums) about these tools for HR AI were found.
Annex III employment obligations moved to 2 December 2027 by law (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744).
Systems placed on the market before that date may continue without new obligations unless materially changed, so incumbent HR-tech products may face little legal pressure.
Near-term risk is commercial rather than regulatory: procurement demands and deals lost to ad hoc answers; later, fines and possible withdrawal or recall of systems.

Employer readiness is low (under 20% very prepared), but use of high-risk HR AI is also limited: 60% of surveyed HR teams use no AI in talent management, and some employers such as Airbus restrict recruiting AI to admin uses in Europe.

Buyer questionnaires ask for risk classification and rationale, Article 11 technical documentation, Article 14 human-oversight design, conformity assessment status, Article 73 incident procedures, fairness or bias audits, and output logs.
Vendors offer shareable bias-audit dashboards as customer-facing evidence.
No evidence shows what an enterprise actually accepted as sufficient; acceptance criteria remain unknown.
